items.title: Google Summer of Code 2026 results
items.author: Jakub Beránek
items.content:
The Rust Project participated in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for the third time this year. This time we had 13 projects, and our dear contributors have been working very hard on them for several months. As usual, the projects had various durations, so while some of them have ended in August, the last one has only finished in November, so we have been waiting until we have all the results before publishing this blog post.

We are very happy to announce that all 13 projects were successful and passed their final evaluation! We consider it to be a testament to the diligence of our contributors, and the helpfulness of our mentors, that we are able to keep a very high rate of successful GSoC projects several years in a row.

At the start of summer, we had a video call with our contributors, so that we could all get to know each other a bit, and learn about their projects. Over the following few months, we continuously communicated with the contributors, provided guidance and answered their questions and reviewed their pull requests. And most importantly, we learned many new things together! It was an overall great experience. We are grateful for all Rust contributions done by our GSoC participants and for the time we spent working together, and we hope that we will continue seeing at least some of them around in the future.

We would like to thank all our Rust GSoC 2026 contributors. You did a great job!

Even though this year we had fewer projects than in 2025, mostly due to limited mentoring capacity, Google Summer of Code 2026 was again a success for the Rust Project. We think that GSoC is a great way of introducing new contributors to our community, and we are looking forward to participating in GSoC (and other mentorship programs, such as Outreachy) again in the near future. If you are interested in becoming a (GSoC) contributor, check out our GSoC project idea list and our guide for new contributors.

Below you can find a brief summary of our GSoC 2026 projects. You can find more information about the original goals of the projects here. For easier navigation, here is an index of the project descriptions in alphabetical order:

And now strap in, as there is a ton of great content to read about here!

A Frontend for Safe GPU Offloading in Rust

Marcelo worked on improving the usability of cross-vendor GPU programs in Rust using the module. At the start of the project, the offload prototype was only a proof of concept. It assumed that the offloaded code was bug-free, and it required users to write a lot of boilerplate code. Marcelo resolved both issues over the summer.

First, he implemented proper type checking. Marcelo extended the compiler to verify that the arguments passed to any offload call are of the correct type, as expected by the GPU kernel. Kernel launches are thus now safe.

After that, he added support for generic kernels. The compiler now collects all generic instantiations launched from the CPU side, and loads that info later when compiling GPU kernels to make sure we instantiate them as needed. Marcelo also added support to select which GPU to use, which is helpful for laptops with both an integrated and a dedicated GPU, as well as for servers with multiple GPUs. He also added two macros that removed the need for any boilerplate when writing and launching GPU kernels.

The hardest part of this project by far was dealing with references. Due to Rust semantics, we cannot just map types containing mutable references to GPUs and then process them using multiple threads. Previous Rust GPU projects used raw pointers as a workaround, but we obviously wanted to avoid those. Marcelo managed to implement a sound abstraction so that users can now safely declare how their kernels will access mutable arguments.

As a cherry on top, Marcelo also ported the RajaPerf performance suite from C++ to Rust and used it to benchmark his pull requests. His safe Rust version matches the performance of the original C++ code, and is now described in a GPU offload paper that he is working on together with his mentor, Manuel. This was Marcelo's second Rust GSoC project, and same as last year, we are very happy with the results. Great job!

Adding WebAssembly Linking Support to Wild

The goal of this project was simple on paper: teach the Wild linker to link WebAssembly (Wasm) programs. However, adding support for a new linker target is of course far from simple. Luckily, Kei already had a lot of experience with Wild, as this was his second GSoC project working on the Wild linker.

And as expected, Kei did a great job! Prior to GSoC 2026, Wild had no Wasm output support. Now, the Wasm support is sufficiently good that Wild can link a range of complex programs to Wasm. For example, it is able to link itself, SQLite, ripgrep, CPython and even the SpiderMonkey JavaScript engine.

And the linking performance is excellent! When compared to , the de-facto standard Wasm linker, which is based on the LLD linker, Wild is 2-15x faster, and uses 2-5x less memory. You can find more benchmarks in his final report, where he also explains that achieving this performance took quite some work, because Wild's ELF linking performance did not immediately translate to being fast when linking Wasm.

Even after this GSoC project ended, Kei has continued improving Wild's Wasm support, as well as contributing to other parts of Wild. Thank you for bringing fast linking to a new set of use-cases, Kei! You are a valued member of the Wild team.

Bringing autodiff and offload into Rust CI

The goal of this project was to build the experimental module, which implements automatic differentiation of Rust code, and the module, which allows offloading Rust code to GPUs, in the CI of the Rust compiler.

Shota has already been contributing to this area in the months leading up to this year's GSoC, so he had no issues getting started. After valiantly fighting with our CI, he made both modules available in the official compiler channel. Rust users can thus now simply install them with a single rustup command, rather than having to compile rustc from source! This is a huge benefit for gathering feedback on these features in the wild, as it makes it much easier to experiment with them.

Beyond making these projects available via rustup, he also worked on making it simpler to build projects that use . The original compilation pipeline was derived from Clang's support for GPU offload, so it involved calling clang helper binaries. That is clearly not optimal, so Shota worked on replacing it by directly calling the underlying LLVM APIs from rustc.

The last piece of his project was enabling testing in CI for both offload and autodiff, which already helped prevent multiple regressions. Right now, the GPU offload pipeline only tests the CPU setup side, but his work allowed us to talk to GPU hardware vendors, two of which already agreed to provide the Rust Project with GPU hardware so that in the future we can also run those tests on dedicated GPUs.

Overall, the project was a success. Shota had to show a lot of patience and endurance when working with various CMake quirks and CI challenges. We would like to extend a special thank you for that!

miri is a tool that can detect undefined behavior (UB) in unsafe Rust code. It used to have a prototype of an interactive debugger called , but it became unmaintained some time ago. The goal of this project was to re-establish , to make it easier to use miri interactively, debug how and why is UB introduced in Rust programs, and also help rustc developers analyse MIR, one of the intermediate representations of Rust programs.

Mohamed successfully reached both main goals of this project. He created a miri interface for the gdb debugger, which allows debugging programs executed by miri. You can set breakpoints, step through individual instructions, analyse MIR local variables and inspect the debugged program's state, with miri acting as a "virtual CPU". So when you encounter your next miri UB report, you can actually debug the program state that caused UB by running ! Mohamed also created a command-line interface for , which is used to test it in miri's CI. This will ensure that it keeps working properly and will not bitrot again.

Mohamed also added basic support for the Debugger Adapter Protocol, which allows using together with IDEs such as Visual Studio Code. Currently, connecting priroda to an IDE is a bit involved, so the next step would be to build a plugin for an IDE that would allow showing all the extra state that miri has, which gdb doesn't know how to interpret.

Debugging programs executed by miri is very exciting. Thank you for all your work!

Implementing impl and mut restrictions

The goal of this project was to implement two new language features that were accepted in RFC 3323:

  • Impl restrictions (), which allow restricting in which modules you are able to implement a given trait.
  • Mut restrictions (struct Foo { pub mut(crate) bar: u8 }), which allow restricting in which modules you are able to mutate a given field.

Ryosuke had to familiarize himself with the compiler's codebase and do a lot of implementation work to get both features working. This included implementing parsing of the new syntax, recording its metadata in the compiler's Abstract Syntax Tree, implementing resolution of the restricted crate paths, and finally adding checks to enforce both restriction rules. This all amounted to around five thousand lines of Rust code!

Once the new features were implemented and available on nightly, Ryosuke wrote a Call for Testing blog post. It had to be very exciting to announce to the world that he implemented two new features from scratch, and people can now play with them on the nightly channel! After the blog post was published, users reported a few issues, which Ryosuke promptly fixed. He also contributed to rustdoc to improve how the impl and mut restrictions are rendered in the generated documentation pages.

Now that the features are available on nightly, feedback is being gathered on them, with the plan being to stabilize them in 2027. If you would like to provide feedback on the impl and mut restrictions, you can do so in this issue.

The goal of this project was clear, and Ryosuke achieved it completely. Awesome work!

Improving Ergonomics and Safety of serialport-rs

The serialport project is a bit different from some other projects which participated in this year's Google Summer of Code. It is more on the side of "facility management" than rocket science. Its challenges are taming finicky operating system APIs and making good abstractions, rather than full-blown software engineering.

Tanmay led many fruitful discussions about potential design decisions, and did a lot of field research on how other crates that depend on serialport actually use its API, to figure out how to make the upcoming breaking API changes less disruptive and painful for them.

Tanmay also worked on sanding off some rough edges of the serialport API, such as replacing Boxed trait objects with enums, and making errors explicit in places where the legacy API used to panic. Some of the work still waits for integration. It is targeting the upcoming serialport 5.0 release.

Christian (Tanmay's mentor) found working alongside Tanmay very motivational, and he was able to catch up with a lot of other unrelated work in order to integrate Tanmay's changes. He noted that working with Tanmay was fun and productive, and that it was pure joy to see him grow from his first contribution in the bonding phase to seasoned contributions. Thank you, Tanmay!

This was my first Google Summer of Code as well. It was challenging, motivating, fun and definitely worth it. I would show up again.

libc: transition differing bit-width time and offset variants and deprecate bug-prone constants

is a foundational crate that is used by thousands of other crates across the Rust ecosystem. For the past several years, its maintainers have been attempting to publish a stable 1.0 release of the crate. Because this crate has to support interoperating with C on many compilation targets with weird quirks, this requires an enormous amount of work. We already had a GSoC project for moving towards 1.0 last year, and the goal of Adam's project was to make more progress in that direction.

And we can happily say that progress was indeed made! The original goal of Adam's project was to deprecate a number of constants that were difficult to maintain and cleanup inconsistencies in handling 32-bit/64-bit variants of file and time handling functions. Adam was able to resolve that in a few weeks, and then he moved on to resolve a number of various issues blocking the 1.0 milestone.

Saying that Adam was productive would be… an understatement. We could follow his work in real-time, because he was posting daily GSoC reports for . The diligence and consistency with which he tackled so many complicated issues was an inspiration to us. In fact, sometimes the reviewers were not able to keep up!

You can find all Adam's pull requests here. You might notice that many of them have lots of comments, and even more discussions happened in GitHub issues and on Zulip. In addition to implementing the necessary code, making changes that affect interesting C platforms and architectures also required him to do a ton of research, and a lot of considerations of edge cases and possible backwards compatibility breakages. His work also took him on a whirlwind tour of diverse platforms; Adam's contributions spanned FreeBSD, NetBSD, Android, Hurd, NuttX, AIX, VxWorks, Fuchsia, L4Re and more.

Even though more work will still be required to get to 1.0, Adam's contributions made a significant dent in this effort. Thank you very much for all your work!

Link Linux kernel and its Modules with Wild

Linker scripts are arcane commands that can be used to instruct a linker to construct the final binary in a custom way. The Wild linker used to implement only basic linker script functionality, which Vishruth greatly expanded during his GSoC project.

Thanks to that, Wild can now successfully link Linux kernel modules, and it's even close to being able to link the Linux kernel itself! Vishruth's work involved greatly expanding expression evaluation support, location counters, program headers, etc. In addition to adding support for many missing bits of linker script support, Vishruth implemented support for partial linking (-r) as this is needed in order to link Linux kernel modules. You can find all the linker script features that he implemented here.

Adding all those peculiar features to Wild required performing many cross-cutting changes to its codebase, which Vishruth managed to do really well. And it was not at the cost of performance! Wild now manages to link Linux kernel modules such as or 2-4x faster than the BFD (GNU ld) or LLD linkers. You can find more benchmarks in his final report.

Vishruth has continued to contribute to Wild even after his GSoC project ended and has become a valued contributor to the project. Thank you very much for making Wild better, Vishruth!

Migrating rust-analyzer assists to SyntaxEditor

rust-analyzer uses rowan for its syntax trees, a library for Concrete Syntax Trees. has served us well over the years, but it has some downsides that cause major performance problems and also smaller convenience issues. In particular, memory fragmentation causes rust-analyzer to consume much more memory than it actually needs (in the order of redundant gigabytes).

We wanted to rewrite to change that. The problem was that many parts in rust-analyzer touch syntax trees, and in particular assists (code actions) of which we have a lot. They also use mutable tree editing, a feature of that can be convenient but was a major obstacle in rewriting it to be more efficient.

During his project, bit-aloo first migrated all rust-analyzer code from mutable tree editing to , a new abstraction that was created specifically to avoid mutation. After that, he removed mutable editing from altogether.

The migration process is incremental and is still inefficient in various aspects. However, we believe that the parts which required changes to large amounts of code are behind us, and we can complete the migration with more focused changes. bit-aloo is continuing to work on that even after his GSoC project ended. And he was also accepted as a member of the rust-analyzer team, so congratulations! We would like to thank him for his work, and hope to continue working with him to improve rust-analyzer for everyone.

Port std::arch test suite to rust-lang/rust

The module of the Rust standard library contains various intrinsic functions that provide architecture and vendor-specific functionality. Their implementation lives in the stdarch repository, which is included as a Josh subtree in the main compiler repo ().

When someone changes the intrinsics in the main repo, breakages can silently creep in, because the main repo does not execute all the tests in its CI. That can cause friction when we synchronize the changes between the two repositories. Ideally, we would run all of 's tests in the main repo to detect any issues as soon as possible.

And that is where Sumit came in! Over the course of his GSoC project, he examined the (very!) complex ways the intrinsics are tested in , and started porting them over to the main repo. But this was not a matter of copying over a few lines of YAML. The compiler repo uses its own build system (called ) and a CI workflow structure that is quite different from the repository. Sumit thus had to first understand what is each test suite doing, reimplement it as a part of bootstrap and finally integrate it into the compiler's CI workflows.

We run ~90 CI jobs across several hardware architectures, operating systems and . Getting all that to work while testing intrinsics required a lot of diligent work… and a lot of patience. It took for one of the test suites to finally succeed on the main repo's CI, and it required Sumit to completely refactor how the suite worked, for it to be more compatible with bootstrap. As another example, a different test suite that Sumit also got to work required running the tests in an Intel CPU emulator on CI.

Sumit ported most of the test suites to , including intrinsics verification against reference implementations, checks for automatically generated source code being up-to-date, and various unit tests for individual intrinsics and CPU feature detection logic. There is one remaining test suite to port, but the ported tests are already helping us find issues, which is great.

You can check Sumit's PRs here; notice that he was also contributing to other parts of Rust in the meantime! Sumit's work will help us make LLVM upgrades and land intrinsics changes more easily. Thank you, Sumit!

Reorganizing tests/ui/issues

The goal of this project was to get rid of a very scary place in the Rust compiler's test suite: a directory called . It contained thousands of test files based on historical Rust issues, dating back all the way to 2012. The problem with those tests was that they were named only with an issue number (e.g. ). When such a test would break, it was quite difficult to figure out what was it even supposed to test, because there was little context attached to it.

Even though we already had a GSoC project to tackle this problem last year, due to the sheer amount of uncategorized tests, there were still over four hundred tests left in this directory by the time zedddie started working on this project.

For each test in this directory, zedddie had to first understand what was the test doing and dig through its original GitHub issue and any other related issues and pull requests. Then they had to figure out what would be the best location to move the test under, search for any possible duplicates, come up with a descriptive name for the test (that tends to be very difficult!), and finally add a short description to the test that explains the context of why the test was added in the first place. Rinse and repeat, for hundreds of tests.

zedddie rolled up their sleeves, and categorized over 300 tests in 30 pull requests. Together with other contributors helping out over this summer, zedddie was finally able to remove the last batch of uncategorized tests at the start of August. As zedddie said in their final report: "What is left to do: nothing, tests/ui/issues is gone".

While this work might sound a bit bland, its positive effect on the maintainability of our test suite, and improving the lives of Rust compiler contributors, is considerable. It is also apparently a great way to learn about cool niche edge cases of Rust that most Rust developers might not know about! After migrating the remaining uncategorized UI tests, zedddie continued contributing to the next trait solver and const generics. Thank you very much for helping us finally get rid of , zedddie!

Utilize debugger APIs to improve debug info test accuracy and error reporting

The Rust debugging experience leaves a lot to be desired. One reason why we struggled to improve it is that many of our debuginfo test suites did not even run in CI for the past few years, as they were difficult to maintain. When something changed in the type visualizers, the implementation details of a standard library type or in debugger internals, someone had to go through tens of tests and manually update them. This was not sustainable, so the test suite rotted.

Luckily for us, Anthony took that affront personally. Even before his GSoC project, he spent considerable effort on improving the quality of debug visualizers of various Rust standard library types, and gained an impressive amount of knowledge about debuggers.

During his GSoC project, he completely overhauled how our debuginfo test infrastructure works, both for LLDB and GDB. Thanks to his improvements, we can now easily "rebless" the reference output when something changes, which makes it much easier to keep our test suite up-to-date. The new tests also record much more information about the internal state of the debugger recorded during the test, which helps with diagnosing issues that cause type visualizers to stop working.

In addition to redesigning the test suite, Anthony also actually managed to re-enable the LLDB tests on both Windows and Linux in our CI again (after several years of being skipped there!). This will allow us to avoid debuginfo regressions and make it easier to improve the Rust debugging experience. Oh, and it goes without saying that while doing all that, he also made numerous improvements to Rust type visualizers. You can find his PRs here.

Anthony's amazing contributions and his deep expertise in debuggers led to him being invited to the Rust Compiler team, which was much deserved. What else can we add, other than: thank you for your awesome work!

XDG path support for rustup

The support for platform-specific directories (platformdirs) has been a long-standing feature request for rustup, to have more fine-grained filesystem directory choices. This project investigated how that issue could be resolved.

The real complexity of this feature request lies within a decade worth of different assumptions that previous iterations of rustup and cargo have made: it turns out that quite a lot of them are no longer true if we were to implement platformdirs support truly faithfully.

Guicheng first worked on cleaning up the interactions between and as a warmup. This issue itself is a very good demonstration of all that compatibility baggage: somehow has become the default binary directory for all things Rust, so rustup ended up installing itself and all its proxies into it. As a result, it has been super annoying to many that everything in is gone with .

After that, he started the actual implementation of platformdirs support in rustup. This was no easy task! Not because the code itself was hard to write, but because it takes a lot of effort to figure out what should be the desired behavior in the first place. Also, in order to determine the appropriate platformdirs semantics, some prior research is often required to see how things became what they are today, so the decoupling of different concerns could proceed, and migration paths could be designed accordingly. It was in this sense that this is different from a typical GSoC project, and luckily thanks to the effort he has put into this project, we have not only come up with the final patch, but also discovered and fixed some tiny preexisting issues with this long-untouched aspect of the rustup codebase along the way.

Thank you for digging into this complex topic, Guicheng!

We would like to thank all contributors who have participated in Google Summer of Code 2026 with us! Your contributions helped make Rust better, and introduced you as new members of our community, which is a reason to celebrate. We are looking forward to participating in GSoC again next year!

We would also like to thank Google for organizing the Google Summer of Code program and for allowing us to host a large number of projects every year. And last, but not least, we would like to thank all the Rust mentors who were tirelessly helping our contributors to complete their projects. Without you, Rust GSoC would not be possible.

items.title: Go Turns 17
items.author: Austin Clements, for the Go team
items.content:
Over the past year, we released Go 1.26 in February and Go 1.27 in August, alongside a steady stream of releases across our libraries and developer tools. Meanwhile, the pace of change across the software industry continues to accelerate, driven by shifting hardware, evolving security threats, and the rapid rise of AI-assisted development and agentic systems.

In a tumultuous time for the industry, Go aims to be a steady hand on the tiller. Our goal is to keep Go grounded in its foundational principles of simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and an unwavering commitment to compatibility, while adapting to modern hardware, production workloads, and developer workflows. Increasingly, our investments serve a : what helps human engineers write, understand, and maintain reliable Go code at scale also provides the guardrails and authoritative context that AI coding assistants and agents need to be effective.

Core language and library improvements

In the language itself, Go 1.26 and 1.27 addressed several long-standing restrictions in generics and everyday Go syntax, guided by years of real-world experience. When generics first landed in Go 1.18, methods could not declare their own type parameters, which sometimes forced awkward package-level functions and “inside-out” nested calls. Go 1.27 introduced generic methods on non-interface types (such as the new method in ), allowing APIs to stay naturally organized on types and enabling readable method chaining. Together with support for self-referential type constraints in Go 1.26 and broader type inference for generic function values in Go 1.27, generics in Go feel more complete and natural than ever.

Alongside generics, two refinements to value construction make everyday Go code cleaner and more concise. Go 1.26 extended the built-in function to accept an initial value expression, allowing or without the ubiquitous -style helper functions used to populate optional pointer fields in JSON and protocol buffer structs. And in Go 1.27, struct literal keys can refer directly to fields of embedded or nested structs, reducing boilerplate in composite literals.

In the standard library, our focus has been on evolving Go’s “production stack” and eliminating subtle operational traps. Few packages are as central to that as , which has been a mainstay of Go since before Go 1.0. While its core model has held up remarkably well for over 15 years, tighter JSON standards and security expectations have turned some of its original defaults into interoperability and security hazards, such as silently accepting invalid UTF-8 or duplicate object keys and matching struct fields case-insensitively. At the same time, its buffered design prevented true streaming and limited performance. Addressing these issues while upholding Go’s compatibility promise for the millions of existing programs that depend on meant designing a new major version of the package.

Six years in the making, the new and packages reached general availability in Go 1.27. Driven by Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, and contributors from across the Go community, this modern JSON API brings safer, stricter defaults, flexible caller- and type-specified customization, and up to 10× faster unmarshaling, while cleanly separating high-level semantic marshaling () from low-level, reflection-free syntactic streaming (). Crucially, we didn’t leave existing code behind: the original package is now implemented entirely in terms of under the hood. Existing callers get faster unmarshaling simply by upgrading, and packages using and interoperate seamlessly so that the ecosystem can migrate gradually without flag days.

We’ve also brought new production diagnostics to Go’s concurrency primitives. Concurrency is one of Go’s greatest strengths, but goroutines accidentally left blocked on abandoned channels or locks can silently leak memory and CPU in long-running services, and traditional goroutine profiles cannot distinguish leaked goroutines from ones legitimately waiting for work. First previewed in Go 1.26 and now generally available in Go 1.27, the new goroutine leak profiler ( in and /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in ) solves this for production services. Contributed by Vlad Saioc and Uber’s Programming Systems team, building on academic research with Aarhus University and Washington University in St. Louis, the profiler repurposes the garbage collector’s reachability phase to identify goroutines blocked on concurrency primitives that no runnable goroutine can ever reach. That allows it to pinpoint leaks in production with near-zero false positives and zero overhead when not in use.

In , closing an HTTP/1 response body with even a single unread byte—such as a trailing newline left behind by a JSON decoder—previously forced the client to tear down the underlying TCP and TLS connection. Go 1.27’s HTTP transport now automatically drains small unread response bodies in the background on close, turning a widespread latency footgun into up to a 5× speedup for sequential HTTP/1 requests while letting application code stay clean and simple.

These releases also added several notable standard library APIs, including a native package, a generic and type-safe , and an in-memory designed for virtual-time testing with . Existing packages saw significant speedups as well: now runs twice as fast while allocating half as much memory, compresses faster (speeding up , , , and ), and has a faster, more accurate encoder and decoder.

Making the most of modern hardware

Modern CPUs look very different from the hardware Go first launched on 17 years ago, with wide vector units and deep, non-uniform memory hierarchies. A major focus of our runtime and compiler work is ensuring Go programs make full use of modern silicon, both transparently when you upgrade your toolchain and through new APIs when you need explicit control.

After debuting as an experiment in Go 1.25, the Green Tea garbage collector became the default in Go 1.26. By organizing object marking around contiguous memory spans rather than chasing pointers across the heap, Green Tea aligns with modern CPU memory architectures to reduce garbage collection overhead by 10–40% in real-world workloads—and by an additional ~10% on recent processors using AVX-512 vector instructions during scanning.

Of course, the runtime shouldn’t be the only part of a Go program that can tap into vector hardware. Without access to Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) capabilities, compute-intensive software, from cryptography and media processing to data analytics and AI, leaves a significant portion of modern silicon dark. Until recently, the only way to light up that hardware in Go was by writing and maintaining per-architecture assembly. To change that, Go 1.26 and 1.27 introduced two experimental SIMD packages: , for low-level access to architecture-specific vector instructions on , (NEON), and WebAssembly (); and , a higher-level, width-agnostic API that provides portable, near-assembly performance across architectures with automatic fallback emulation.

We’ve also attacked the cost of memory allocation from multiple angles. The cheapest heap allocation is the one that never happens: in Go 1.26, the compiler began allocating initial slice backing stores on the stack at sites—even for slices that ultimately escape to the heap—eliminating the flurry of small heap allocations that typically accompany slice growth. And for heap allocations more broadly, Go 1.27 introduced size-specialized memory allocation to speed up allocating the small objects (such as small structs, slices, and strings) that dominate allocator time. Generating dedicated fast-path allocator routines for size classes up to 80 bytes made small allocations up to 30% faster and improved overall performance in allocation-heavy programs. Together with a ~30% reduction in baseline call overhead in Go 1.26, these improvements make Go programs faster and leaner out of the box.

Secure software and ecosystem defense

Go’s approach to security spans the entire lifecycle of software: providing safe APIs by design, preparing cryptography for the future, and actively defending the live ecosystem as new threats emerge.

To defend against store-now, decrypt-later attacks and support the industry’s accelerating timelines for quantum readiness, Go has continued expanding its post-quantum cryptography support. Go 1.26 enabled hybrid post-quantum key exchanges ( and ) by default in and added the package (implementing RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption, including post-quantum hybrid KEMs). Go 1.27 followed up with the new package, implementing the FIPS 204 post-quantum ML-DSA signature standard and integrating it into and .

At the same time, we’ve continued hardening the standard library and runtime against subtle classes of vulnerabilities. Most key generation and signing functions across Go’s packages now unconditionally draw from a secure system randomness source, closing off a classic footgun where non-cryptographic readers were accidentally passed in. Under the hood, Go 1.26 also added 64-bit heap base address randomization to harden binaries and introduced the experimental package for eagerly erasing sensitive cryptographic temporaries from registers, stack frames, and the heap.

Securing Go deployments also requires rapid vulnerability and incident response in a fast-moving threat landscape. From the Go vulnerability database and to our release infrastructure, we’ve invested heavily in ecosystem defense. In October, that preparation was put to the test during the eMudhra certificate key disclosure incident, when eight intermediate TLS and code-signing certificates chaining to a widely trusted root CA were discovered to use trivially weak private keys. Because Linux lacks a uniform OS-level certificate revocation mechanism, Go’s built-in TLS verifier is the frontline defense for millions of Linux services. Within seven and a half hours of initial notification, the Go Security team shipped a targeted block in our first-ever URGENT track security release (Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10) alongside an updated Go vulnerability database entry so could flag affected binaries, giving Go users everything they needed to protect their deployments before the weak keys were publicly disclosed the next morning.

Go has always been more than a compiler and standard library: it is an end-to-end platform for software engineering. Over the past year, our work in , the language server, , and has focused on making that platform even more productive for both human developers and AI coding assistants.

In last fall’s Go Developer Survey, the single biggest challenge developers reported was ensuring their code follows best practices and current Go idioms. As Go evolves while standing by its compatibility promise, older ways of writing code continue to work alongside newer, clearer, or faster alternatives, creating a natural drift in idioms over time. That drift has been compounded by AI coding assistants, which gravitate toward the older patterns that dominate their training data.

Go 1.26 tackled this with a complete overhaul of the command, returning the long-dormant tool to its pre-Go 1.0 roots to apply dozens of automatic across entire codebases. What did for stylistic consistency, modernizers aim to do for idiomatic consistency. Available both as instant suggestions in and as bulk, push-button upgrades in , modernizers simplify existing code and help developers discover new language and library features. We now routinely consider whether new language and library proposals should ship with a modernizer of their own. Just as importantly, modernizers give coding agents an immediate way to bring generated code up to date, while helping shift the global corpus of open source Go code so that future models learn modern idioms from the start.

Bespoke modernizers work well for the language and standard library, but a centralized team can never write them for every third-party module in the ecosystem. That’s why Go 1.26 also introduced the annotation-driven source-level inliner, the first step toward a “self-service” paradigm for automated code maintenance. Any package author can now annotate a deprecated function, type, or constant with , and the inliner will safely migrate callers and references via or in the IDE, carefully handling evaluation order, side effects, and name shadowing.

In the editor, we’ve made four feature-packed releases of over the past year (v0.21.0, v0.22.0, v0.23.0, and v0.24.0). In collaboration with the Dart team, we designed and proposed an open Language Server Protocol (LSP) extension for interactive refactoring, allowing language servers to ask for user input through dynamic, multi-step dialogs in any supporting editor. Now integrated into and , interactive refactoring powers customizable struct tag addition and removal, interface implementation (including generic interfaces) with live symbol search, and cross-package declaration moves. Beyond refactoring, also gained generalized package renaming across directories, zero-configuration support for editing Go assembly files, subexpression hover inspection, completions and inlay hints for promoted fields, automatic scanning when dependencies change, and continued enhancements to its built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI coding assistants.

Rounding out the developer platform, in May we launched the official API and followed up with support for in Go 1.27. Previously, developer tools and IDE integrations had to resort to fragile web scraping to query ecosystem metadata. Today, the API gives tool authors and AI coding agents a fast, authoritative service for querying module versions, package symbols, importers, and vulnerability data, while makes it easy to pull up documentation for any version of any package right from the command line.

We have an ambitious year ahead for Go.

On the tooling front, we’re building on the API, , and to make Go’s developer tools even more capable for both human developers and coding agents. Following the strong community response to and , we’re exploring ways to expand self-service static analysis, enabling developers, package maintainers, and organizations to easily integrate custom analyzers and domain-specific best-practice checks directly into their development workflows. We’re also exploring ways to surface richer package health and quality signals on and through its API, helping developers and coding agents evaluate and choose trustworthy, reliable dependencies.

In the language and libraries, Go 1.28 will resolve one of Go’s longest-standing language requests by allowing composite literals to omit redundant types whenever the type can be inferred from context, cutting visual noise in deeply nested configurations, API requests, and table-driven tests. And with recent generics refinements and hashing APIs in place, we’ve just accepted a swath of proposals for generic collection APIs—including sets, ordered maps, and more—which will land in over the next few weeks so the community can try them out and share feedback ahead of future standard library inclusion.

Under the hood, we’re working hard to graduate a large subset of the and packages (covering , NEON, and ) in Go 1.28, with further expansions and scalable vector (SVE) support targeted for Go 1.29. Amid the global RAM crunch, reducing Go’s memory footprint is also one of our major priorities for the coming year.

Finally, ensuring Go stands the test of time means scaling not just our technology, but the open source project itself. Over the past year, some of Go’s most impactful advances, including and the profile, were driven by or built in close partnership with contributors outside Google. To better support our growing ecosystem and contributor base, we’re working to bridge the gap between Go maintainers at Google and our broader community, and to diversify Go’s technical stewardship. That includes restructuring the proposal process to improve throughput, give the community clearer visibility into the process and input into prioritization, and formally involve community contributors in triage and review. Beyond proposals, we are building a clearer contributor ladder to empower proven contributors with greater autonomy, decision-making privileges, and maintenance responsibilities, and opening up maintainer summits and day-to-day communications to trusted contributors from our amazing community.

Seventeen years in, Go is thriving because of the people who use it, build with it, and contribute to it every day. Thank you to everyone in the Go community for being part of this journey, and we wish you all the best in the year ahead!
